Artificial turf replacement in Kissimmee, Florida

Artificial turf replacement means pulling out a worn-out lawn, correcting the base underneath it, and laying a new surface, usually once a lawn is ten to fifteen years into Florida's sun. A full tear-out and rebuild prices close to a new install; a sound base that only needs the old turf removed trims a meaningful share off that. Most jobs also bring an older install up to the current state turf standard.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Repair or replace? What the base tells you

Artificial turf replacement means old turf removal, a base rebuild where it's needed, honest turf disposal, and a re-turf that upgrades the product you had rather than a like-for-like swap. The condition of what's underneath, not just how the lawn looks, is what should decide between a repair and a full replacement.

Repair or replace: reading the signs
What you seeRepair candidateReplace candidateWhy
A single open seam or a small burn patchYesNot necessaryIsolated failure; the rest of the base and turf are still sound
Widespread fading and brittle blades across the whole lawnNo, a patch won't matchYesThe fiber itself has UV-degraded; that doesn't repair, it only gets replaced
Multiple soft, sunken or spongy spots at 12+ years oldRarely worth itUsuallyThe base has likely failed in more than one place, not only where it shows
Pet odor that survives a deep clean and fresh infillNoYesOften means the backing or an old fabric weed barrier underneath is holding urine
Turf installed before the 2026 state standard, irrigation still capped underneathN/AWorth doing at the same timeReplacement is the practical moment to remove old heads and anchor edges to the current rule

What survives a replacement, and what doesn't

A base that's still flat, well-drained and at the right depth doesn't need to be dug out and redone; that's the single biggest cost difference between a replacement and a first-time install. We probe it in a few spots, check for soft or wet areas, and reuse what's still doing its job while adding and recompacting where it's thinned. Edging often survives too. A bender-board or paver border holds up longer than the turf inside it, so a still-solid edge gets reused rather than pulled for no reason.

What doesn't survive: the turf itself, obviously, along with any fabric weed barrier from an older pet install, since that's usually the thing holding years of urine odor. Old irrigation heads that were simply capped rather than removed get addressed properly this time, since the current standard doesn't allow an in-ground system to water turf at all. Infill is the other thing worth checking before assuming it can stay: the current state standard only allows crumb rubber or another synthetic infill inside the footprint of playground equipment, so an older lawn or general play area filled with rubber or TPE gets refilled with clean silica sand, zeolite or a coated sand during the replacement.

Ten to fifteen years of Florida sun, up close

Turf in Florida generally lasts ten to twenty years depending on UV stabilization, traffic and infill (industry lifespan data), and the low end of that range is common on unshaded Central Florida lawns that see full sun most of the year. What worn-out looks like by then: blades gone from green to a washed-out gray-green, brittle rather than springy underfoot; infill migrated or compacted so the backing shows through in traffic lanes; a surface that's stopped bouncing back after someone walks across it.

A lawn that hit those marks five years ago and is only now getting replaced usually has base problems layered on top of the fiber problems, part of why the quote is rarely just the cost of new material. This guide breaks lifespan down by use and product.

How a replacement job runs

The sequence differs from a first-time install mainly in the first step.

  1. We evaluate what's underneath first. Pull back a corner, probe the base for depth and moisture, and decide how much of it is worth keeping before pricing anything.
  2. Old turf comes out. Cut into sections, rolled, and hauled off; a large yard can mean several thousand pounds of material leaving the site.
  3. The base gets corrected, not just reused blindly. Low spots are regraded, thinned base gets built back up, and the whole area is recompacted in lifts even where most of it stayed.
  4. New turf goes in to the current standard. A product with no intentionally added PFAS or heavy metals, edges and seams anchored the way Rule 62-308.100 requires.
  5. Irrigation is capped properly. Any head that survived the old install, even one that was already turned off, gets capped at the line rather than left in place.
  6. Final grade and drainage check. We confirm the 1 to 2 percent slope away from the house still holds before the last section of turf goes down.

What artificial turf replacement costs

Artificial turf replacement is quoted per job rather than off a fixed rate, but it prices closer to a first-time install than to a repair, because most of the labor, demo, base work, new turf, repeats either way. A full tear-out and rebuild often lands near the lower-to-middle part of the usual Central Florida installed range, roughly $8–$18 a square foot, and a base that only needs light correction can trim a meaningful share off that.

What raises it: hauling a large volume of old turf and infill off site, a base that failed in more than one area, and capping or rerouting irrigation left in place under the old lawn. What lowers it: a base that's still flat and draining, sound edging that doesn't need to be pulled, and a straightforward rectangular yard.

Where the old turf actually goes

Turf is technically recyclable; plastics can be separated, melted and repelletized. In practice, most residential turf in Florida is hauled to a landfill or a construction-and-demolition debris facility, the same as old carpet, because separating fiber, backing and infill takes equipment most local waste operations don't run (an industry overview of turf recycling). We haven't found a synthetic-turf recycling program serving Central Florida as of September 2026. Landfilling isn't an oversight the state rule ignores, either: Rule 62-308.100 requires turf, backing and infill to be disposable at a Florida-permitted landfill under normal conditions, which is exactly where most of it ends up. Disposal is typically priced by weight; national guides put it around $60 to $70 a ton (a synthetic grass disposal guide), and a mid-size residential lawn's worth of old turf and infill adds up to a real number, part of a replacement quote rather than an afterthought.

Bringing an older install up to the current rule

A lot of turf around Kissimmee went in before Florida adopted Rule 62-308.100 on May 19, 2026, the first statewide minimum standard for synthetic turf on single-family lots (Rule 62-308.100). Replacement is the natural moment to catch an older lawn up: a product with no intentionally added PFAS or heavy metals, a washed and open-graded base instead of whatever was under the original install, edges and seams anchored to handle wind and flooding, and irrigation heads capped rather than left running under the turf. If the old install sits inside a live oak's drip line, or closer than ten feet to a pond or canal without a seawall or bulkhead between them, replacement is also the moment to correct that footprint instead of repeating it. On a Poinciana or Harmony lot with a septic system, we also confirm the new layout leaves the tank's lid reachable for pump-out, easy to overlook on an install built before the rule existed.

None of this requires a new permit from the state. Rule 62-308.100 sets a material and installation standard, and it says outright that it creates no new department-issued permit and doesn't touch easements or rights-of-way; what changed is what a compliant lawn has to look like, not who has to sign off on it.

HOA paperwork the second time around

An HOA that approved the original install years ago may still want to see the new one, especially if the community's design guidelines changed in the meantime or the visible footprint is different. What a Florida HOA can and can not restrict explains that a fenced backyard is generally protected from that review under F.S. 720.3045, while a front yard isn't. We prepare a fresh sample, spec sheet and site plan for the file when a community asks for one, same as on a first-time install.

What a bad replacement job looks like

The most common shortcut is skipping the base evaluation entirely and laying new turf over whatever's there, wet spots, soft spots and all, so the new lawn inherits the old lawn's problems on day one. Reusing edging that's already failed, cracked bender board, a paver border that's settled, saves a little money and costs more within a year when the new turf's edge lifts along it. Leaving old irrigation lines simply capped with tape instead of properly plugged is a leak waiting for the first hard rain to find it.

After the new turf goes down

Treat a replacement's first few months like a new install: keep heavy furniture off it while the base settles, rinse and brush on the same schedule as before, and walk the perimeter after the first real storm to check that every edge and seam is holding. Keep the product's spec sheet and the invoice describing the base work done; useful if an HOA ever asks again, and useful to us if a question comes up later about what's under the new lawn.

Who is the best artificial turf replacement company near me?

Ask to see the base before it's covered; a contractor confident in the work will show you the compacted material and the grade before the last roll of turf goes down. Ask what happens to the old turf and whether disposal is itemized in the quote. And ask directly whether the new install will meet the current state standard, anchored edges, capped irrigation, a PFAS-free product, since that's a fair baseline for anyone replacing turf in Florida now, not an upsell.

We'll look at what's underneath before pricing anything, and tell you honestly if a repair would do instead.

Questions people ask

How do I know if my base needs to be rebuilt or just corrected?

We probe it in several spots with a rod or a shovel. Firm, dry material that hasn't shifted usually just needs recompacting; soft, wet or spongy material in more than one spot means the base itself has failed and needs to come out and be rebuilt.

Can the old turf be reused anywhere, like a dog run or a shed pad?

Rarely for anything load-bearing or visible; UV-degraded fiber is brittle and the backing is usually near the end of its life too. It occasionally works as a temporary weed barrier under mulch, but that's a stretch, not a real second life.

Does replacement turf need a permit if the original install didn't?

Usually not a building permit, since it's the same use of the lot, but check with your city or county if the project also changes grading or drainage. An HOA that reviewed the first install may want to see the new one even without a government permit involved.

How long does a typical replacement take?

Two to five days for a residential yard, depending on how much of the base needs correcting. A yard where the base only needs light recompaction moves closer to a first-time install's timeline; one needing a full rebuild takes longer.

Will a replacement match the rest of my landscaping if only part of the yard is worn out?

We can often match pile height and color family to an adjoining area that's staying, though turf from a different production run is never a perfect color match. Full-yard replacement avoids the mismatch question entirely.

Is it cheaper to replace turf myself and just hire out disposal?

Removing the old turf yourself can trim some labor cost, but the base correction underneath is the part that determines how the new lawn performs, and that's harder to get right without the equipment and experience to grade and compact it properly.

Does homeowners insurance ever cover turf replacement?

Sometimes, for storm or fire damage specifically, rarely for ordinary wear from age and sun. Check your policy's language on landscaping or outdoor improvements before assuming either way, and keep the original install invoice in case a claim needs it.
